# Methods

### Flow chart of data preparation / collection

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A[define genera of interest] -->|get accession numbers| B(download accession metadata)
  B -->|get genomic information| C(download .fasta information)
  C --> D[convert genomic data to protein data]
  D --> E[combine fastas into large files]
  E --> F(perform eggnog-mapper search)
  F --> G(perform eggnog-mapper annotation)
  G --> H(perform KEGG enrichment)
  H --> I{{perform analysis}}
  B -->|enrich data for analyses| I
```

## **Clean up and compress files**

Once I got onto hawk I saw that I had a lot of files left over from work done in Year 2. I wanted to download all of these to my OneDrive for safekeeping and then clear down my home folder on hawk, to create space and generally make it easier to navigate.

To make them a bit easier to download, I wanted to compress them and combine them to the smallest possible size.

I already had two folders called archive\_\<date\> and then I created a third one, for today, and put everything else in it. Using the command `du -sh *` I could see that the third archive was very large, so I dealt with that separately as shown below. (this command gives the "real" size of directories, as on hawk, all directories say they take up "4096")

### **Smaller archive folders**

I used the following to compress each one:

`tar -cf - ./<folder name> | xz -9ve > <archive_name>.tar.xz`

It is quite a slow process; a 5GB directly took 90 mins to compress to 4.2G - hardly worth it really.

### **Larger archive folder**

Inside the archive folder I created today there are a lot of annotations folders from eggNOG-mapper. Each one isn’t huge but together they combine to nearly 9.5GB.

For these, I created separate folders so that folders with similar accession numbers (e.g. GCF_0001xxx or GCA_0001xxx) are grouped together in a folder with that prefix, using this script:

`if [ -d "$dir" ]; then`\
`digits=$(echo "$dir" | sed 's/GCA_\([0-9]\{4\}\).*/\1/')`\
`prefix="GCA_$digits"`\
`mkdir -p "$prefix"`\
`mv "$dir" "$prefix/"`\
`echo "Moved $dir to $prefix/"`\
`fi`\
`done`

Then I compressed them in batches like this:

`for dir in GCF_0011 GCF_0012 GCF_0013 GCF_0014 GCF_0015; do`\
`[ -d "$dir" ] && tar -cf - "$dir" | xz -9ev > "${dir}.tar.xz" && echo "Compressed $dir"`\
`done`

## **Creating and running R Script on Hawk**

I used code Claude.ai provided to create a file that loads one of the existing rds files and prints the first 3 list elements. This file is called "test_command_line.R". I used `vi` to create the actual file on hawk, into which I put the code. (As this was just a little test, I was a bit more lenient on my use of AI to code for me)

When I tried to run the command `Rscript` I got an error to say the program wasn’t known; I need to load R first. I used:

`module avail R` to list all R versions on hawk and then:\
`module load R/4.4.2`

To run the R script I need to pass in the location of the rds file which it loads. With no .proj file in use on Hawk, I have to pass the complete path relative to where I am, i.e.

`Rscript 00_scripts/R_scripts/test_command_line.R 01_inputs/03_metadata/taxonomy_information_Sphingomonas_Brevibacterium_Microbacterium_Brachybacterium_Pantoea_2025-09-10.rds`

## **Save to git**

I then needed to stage, commit and push my changes back to the github repo. To do this, I had to create a [personal access token](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens) on github first - you do this by selecting the settings option under your profile picture, not settings in the repo.

I then also had to set up some git config before I could commit:

`git config --global user.email "toby.nunn.uk@outlook.com"`\
`git config --global user.name "Tobias Nunn"`

To view what had changed, I typed `git status`. To stage everything I typed `git add *` although I think it is actually meant to be `git add .`.

Then to commit the change I typed `git commit -m "Test script for running on hawk command line"`\
And finally to push I typed `git push origin main`. Mobaxterm opened up a dialog box that prompted me for my git username and my password, into which I put my personal access token. I then went and checked github desktop and the push was successful, so that all works.

Now that I am done with that mini-section, I will test running R on hawk from a slurm script. This may be useful because I will likely want to call the script that collects all of the .fasta files from slurm. This is because it is resource intensive, and slurm is the way of handling stuff like that on hawk. I will do this by modifying that "test_command_line.R" script to output to a file.

I modified and tested the file on my machine first, then pushed them to the github repo. A step of note was using Notepad++ to turn all the carriage returns into Unix style, which does have an impact when on Hawk. Syncing with the repo was as simple as running `git pull` and then a `git status` to check it worked.

### Running R through Slurm on Hawk

Running the modified "test_command_line.R" file was very simple. It is run through a slurm script called "R_from_slurm.sh". It was very similar to running the base R script from the terminal in R studio. The exact code was:

`sbatch R_from_slurm.sh ~/source/01_inputs/03_metadata/taxonomy_information_Sphingomonas_Brevibacterium_Microbacterium_Brachybacterium_Pantoea_2025-09-10.rds`

To note, sbatch is how to call slurm, \~ is needed on hawk as this makes it default to the home directory

To check how the job was doing, I ran the commands:

-   `squeue -u b.tbn23vlc`

-   `scontrol show job 59931057`

It took 5 seconds to complete, and once it was done, the output file of "output.txt" was in my home directory on hawk. In conclusion, it is very viable to run an R script through a slurm script on hawk.

The code inside "R_from_slurm.sh" can be found [here.](https://github.com/tobiasnunn/undergrad_dissertation/blob/12e9a845f20377b0b2cfe99ecffc8b318cabcfa7/00_scripts/Slurm_scripts/R_from_slurm.sh)

NEXT STEPS: Now I am ready to begin construction of my .fasta getting script.

In the "NCBI_functions" script, I created a 4th function that takes a user input of either "genome", "protein" or "both", as well as an accession. It uses these specifications to run a call to an NCBI API endpoint. It stores this result and moves it around until it outputs the desired fasta content as a list into an object in my "04_fastafile_getter.R" script.

I have created a new directory for this fasta information under "01_inputs/04_fastas/". Because this area is going to get rather humungous with the amount of fastas I plan to download, I have placed this directory in the .gitignore, excluding it from making it up to the repo.

I updated the "04_fastafile_getter.R" script to now run a for loop where a vector of accession names are read in, the function is then run and the result is saved out as an rds file inside the loop. They are about 2MB each, and fasta files held raw are about 5-6MB each, so for each fasta I save as rds, I am saving about 3-4MB, multiply by like 5000 accessions and I am saving somewhere between 15 and 20GB
